description: Team for "Dancing with the SARs". We're a family of Robotics, AI and IT engineering enthusiasts, building an interactive app that uses NASA-ISRO NISAR radar to show real surface change checked against reported events.
summary: MonsoonLens is an open web app that shows what the NASA-ISRO NISAR radar saw around Pune, India, during the July 2026 monsoon. From 3 to 8 July, floods and landslides hit the district while NASA's daily satellite images showed only cloud. NISAR's L-band radar sees through cloud, so we compared its passes of 28 June and 10 July and mapped new water and likely landslide zones on the Western Ghats slopes. We then checked the map against 18 reported events and show, on screen, what the radar missed and why. It addresses the challenge with an interactive NISAR application for one real event, with time steps, polarisations and physical drivers explained. It matters because cloud hides the ground exactly when people need to see it.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

MonsoonLens has six pages, a one-minute guided tour, and works in English, Hindi, Marathi and German, on a phone or a computer. The Overview gives the findings, the checks and a 3D view. The Story walks through six steps: the rain, why radar, before and after, what changed, the weeks after, and what radar could not see, with a before-and-after slider on the radar images. The Explore map lets you switch layers and base maps, filter slide zones by confidence, click any zone or reported event to see its details and source, and download the results. Check a place lets anyone pick one of 431 villages and towns and see what was found within 2, 5 or 10 km. The Field check list ranks every likely slide zone with its radar evidence and what is nearby, as a printable list and KML for phones. The Method page lists every NISAR file, every threshold, every check and every limit.

WHAT WE FOUND

- 8.5 km² of new water where Pune's reservoirs and rivers rose between 28 June and 10 July.

- 0.36 km² of flood water, in 30 patches, still standing on 10 July on ground where no water was recorded between 1984 and 2021.

- 50 likely slide zones on steep slopes, 8 of them high confidence. They are leads to check, not confirmed landslides: 46 have no reported event within 2 km.

- Over the season, open water in rivers and reservoirs grew from 130 km² on 28 June to 186 km² on 14 October as the reservoirs filled (five NISAR passes on the same track and mode).

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline reads only the Pune box from each NISAR file, on a 40 m grid.

- New water: pixels that are dark in HH on 10 July but not on 28 June, at least 3 dB darker, on flat ground, outside permanent water. The dark/bright threshold is learned for each date from known reservoirs and known dry land.

- Likely slide zones: slopes of 15° to 45° where radar coherence between the two passes is low and the brightness changed (HH up by 3 dB or more, or HV down by 2 dB or more).

- Rainfall (GPM IMERG) shows the cause; permanent water and slope come from public maps.

- The app reads only small precomputed files, so it loads quickly on a phone.

HOW WE CHECKED IT

- Against reports: 18 events from news sources, each linked. Of 10 floods radar could observe, 3 had a "possible water" patch nearby, which is no better than chance: places nobody reported match about 3.8 of 10 under the same rule. The 7 misses were all reported in or near towns, where radar echoes off walls can hide street flooding; that is a likely reason, not one we measured. Of 7 landslides we could locate, radar could observe 4; we matched 2, both to the same zone.

- Against a second orbit: NISAR track 106 (3 to 15 July) saw 12 of the zones and found 2 again, about 8 times what chance gives (p = 0.026).

- Against a second elevation map: re-run with NASA's NASADEM, 35 of the 50 zones are found again, 7 of the 8 high-confidence ones. The two landslide matches do not hold in that run, and we say so.

- Against cloud: all 22 available NASA daily true-colour images of the area for 3 to 8 July are fully cloud-covered.

WHAT RADAR COULD NOT SEE

Flooded streets between buildings; water that came and went between passes; slides smaller than a 40 m pixel or on gentle ground; the 2% of steep ground hidden from the radar; and the fact that NISAR products are still provisional. These limits are on the Overview page, not in a footnote.

BENEFITS AND WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

A district disaster office could see where the ground changed within days of a storm, without field access, and know how far to trust the map. Road and rail operators on the ghat sections get a list of slopes to inspect. The same code runs on any pair of NISAR passes for any district, so the next step is to run it automatically for each new pass over the Western Ghats.

TOOLS

Python (h5py, rasterio, pyproj, shapely, SciPy, NumPy, pandas, earthaccess), Streamlit, folium, deck.gl (3D view), Plotly, Pillow, pytest, GitHub, Streamlit Community Cloud. Code licence: MIT.
